#### Skew, a guessing watermark, and what completeness costs

**What is being answered.** Why a watermark is a guess, and what the guess costs — as three functions over the same 9 events.

`watermarkAfter(i)` only ever reads `EVENTS[0..i]`. That single fact is the whole limitation: it is arithmetic over what arrived, so it **cannot** account for something that has not arrived. Step 1 catches it making a false claim with no error path available to it.

`waitFor(events, budget)` then shows that completeness is purely a matter of the `budget` argument — and `priceOf` converts that argument into the latency every window pays. The two together are the trade, with numbers on both sides.

The animation steps through the code, holding each line long enough to read the STACK (call frames and their locals) and the HEAP (allocated arrays and objects) as they are AT THAT MOMENT. Expand any step to study it on its own.

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch01-eventtime-memory/ch01-eventtime-memory.svg" alt="Skew, a guessing watermark, and what completeness costs, 4 steps showing stack and heap" width="980">

<details>
<summary><b>Step 1 of 4</b> — the watermark claims a time is settled when it is not</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch01-eventtime-memory/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: the watermark claims a time is settled when it is not" width="980">

`seen` is the highest event time in the first 8 events — 260s — so the claim is 260 − 60 = 200. That asserts nothing earlier than 12:03:20 can still arrive. id 7, at 12:00:50, is arriving right now. The claim is false and the function has no way to know.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — waiting 60s: id 7 falls on the wrong side</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch01-eventtime-memory/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: waiting 60s: id 7 falls on the wrong side" width="980">

`skewOf(EVENTS[7])` is 230, and `budget` is 60, so 230 > 60 and the event is dropped. 8 of 9 events are kept. Note what decided it: one comparison against a number a human typed.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — waiting 230s: the same call keeps everything</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch01-eventtime-memory/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: waiting 230s: the same call keeps everything" width="980">

Same function, `budget` = 230, and `dropped` comes back empty. Completeness is available — it was never a question of algorithms. And 230 is exactly `max(skewOf(e))` over the whole dataset, which is a number you can only compute once every event has already arrived.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — and the bill for that completeness</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch01-eventtime-memory/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: and the bill for that completeness" width="980">

`priceOf(230).delayTotal` is 230 × 4 = 920s against 60 × 4 = 240s, so `extra` = 680s. That is the exchange rate: 680 seconds of added delay to stop losing 1 event in 9. No one can compute whether that trade is worth making.

</details>
